### Data Quality Controls  
The foundation of any trustworthy risk score is high‑fidelity input data. Each hospital’s EHR must feed the model through a standardized interface that validates source integrity (e.g., HL7/FHIR conformance), checks for missingness or outliers, and applies consistent coding standards such as LOINC for laboratory values and SNOMED CT for clinical observations. A central data‑quality dashboard should flag drift in key variables—such as changes in the distribution of lactate levels or vital‑sign capture rates—that could bias predictions. Regular audits (quarterly) of de‑identified patient subsets can surface systematic errors, while automated bias‑detection scripts assess whether model performance differs across protected characteristics (age, sex, race). ---

### Model Validation Protocols  
Before clinical rollout, the sepsis risk score should undergo multi‑step validation. First, a retrospective cohort study across all 12 sites must demonstrate acceptable discrimination (AUROC ≥ 0.80) and calibration (Hosmer–Lemeshow p > 0.05). Subgroup analyses—by age group, comorbidity burden, and ICU vs general ward—are essential to detect performance heterogeneity that could translate into inequitable care. Second, a prospective pilot in a subset of hospitals should evaluate real‑time predictive accuracy against the SSC sepsis bundle outcomes (e.g., time to antibiotics). The FDA’s 2024 AI/ML SaMD guidance recommends documenting training data provenance, version control, and risk‑based post‑market monitoring plans; these documents must be archived for regulatory review. Finally, a formal “clinical validation study” that meets the criteria of a prospective, randomized controlled trial (RCT) is ideal but not always feasible for early deployments; in such cases, a quasi‑experimental design with matched controls can provide credible evidence.

---

### Real‑Time Monitoring  
Once live, the system must feed into an operational dashboard that tracks key performance indicators: sensitivity at 90 % specificity, false‑positive rate per 1,000 patient days, and alert latency. A statistical process control chart (e.g., Shewhart or EWMA) can detect shifts in these metrics that signal model drift or data quality issues. A dedicated “alert‑review” workflow should capture clinician feedback (e.g., override reasons) and feed this data back into periodic model retraining cycles. Incident reporting mechanisms must be in place so that any adverse events potentially linked to the AI score are captured, investigated, and reported to the FDA’s MedWatch system if required.

---

### Workflow Integration Strategies  
Embedding the risk score within the existing EHR interface is critical for clinician trust. The tool should appear as a contextual pop‑up within the patient summary screen, accompanied by a concise explanation of the underlying probability (“Sepsis Risk = 0.42”) and recommended next steps (e.g., “Order lactate, start broad‑spectrum antibiotics”).
